learningObjectives.title: The Bolsheviks in power and civil war
Stalin's rule: collectivisation, the Five-Year Plans and the purges

questions.q: In which month and year did Tsar Nicholas II abdicate the throne?
questions.explain: Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917 during the February Revolution, ending over 300 years of Romanov rule.

questions.q: Which slogan is associated with Lenin's April Theses of 1917?
questions.explain: Lenin's April Theses promised 'Peace, Bread, Land' and 'All Power to the Soviets', winning popular support for the Bolsheviks.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'dual power' that existed in Russia after February 1917?
options: Power was shared between the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet
The Tsar ruled jointly with his son Alexei
Russia was governed by both a king and a president
The Bolsheviks and Mensheviks controlled the army together
questions.explain: After the Tsar's abdication, authority was split between the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet, weakening effective rule.

questions.q: Who became the leader of the Provisional Government by the autumn of 1917?
questions.explain: Alexander Kerensky led the Provisional Government by autumn 1917 but was overthrown by the Bolsheviks in October.

questions.q: Why did the Kornilov Revolt of 1917 strengthen the Bolsheviks?
options: Kerensky armed the Bolshevik Red Guards to help defend Petrograd
The Bolsheviks captured the Winter Palace during the revolt
It forced the Tsar to return to power
questions.explain: To resist Kornilov's advance on Petrograd, Kerensky armed the Bolsheviks, boosting their strength and popularity.

questions.q: An eyewitness describes armed Red Guards storming the Winter Palace and arresting the Provisional Government's ministers. Which event is being described?
questions.explain: The storming of the Winter Palace and the arrest of Provisional Government ministers took place during the Bolshevik seizure of power in October 1917.

questions.q: Which 1918 treaty took Russia out of the First World War?
questions.explain: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918) ended Russia's involvement in the war but forced it to surrender large amounts of territory to Germany.

questions.q: Why did Lenin dissolve the Constituent Assembly in January 1918?
options: The Bolsheviks had failed to win a majority of the seats
The Assembly voted to restore the Tsar
The building had been destroyed by fire
questions.explain: The Socialist Revolutionaries won most seats, so Lenin closed the Assembly after one day to keep the Bolsheviks in control.

questions.q: Who was the head of the Cheka, the Bolshevik secret police?
questions.explain: Felix Dzerzhinsky led the Cheka, which used the Red Terror to crush opponents of the Bolshevik regime.

questions.q: A civil war poster praises the Commissar for War who organised and led the Red Army to victory. Which Bolshevik leader does it depict?
questions.explain: As Commissar for War, Trotsky created and commanded the Red Army, playing a key role in the Bolshevik victory in the Civil War.

questions.q: What was the main aim of the policy of War Communism during the Civil War?
options: To supply the Red Army and the cities by requisitioning grain from peasants
To allow peasants to sell surplus grain for profit
To encourage foreign investment in Russian industry
To hand factories back to their former owners
questions.explain: War Communism forcibly requisitioned grain and nationalised industry to feed the Red Army and urban workers during the Civil War.

questions.q: In which year did the Kronstadt sailors rebel against Bolshevik rule?
questions.explain: The 1921 Kronstadt Rebellion by once-loyal sailors alarmed Lenin and helped persuade him to abandon War Communism.

questions.q: By 1921 food production had collapsed, famine threatened, and even loyal sailors had rebelled. Which policy did Lenin introduce in response?
questions.explain: Faced with economic collapse and unrest, Lenin introduced the NEP in 1921, allowing peasants to sell surplus grain and permitting some private trade.

questions.q: What happened to Tsar Nicholas II and his family in July 1918?
options: They were executed by the Bolsheviks
They escaped into exile in Britain
They were imprisoned but later released
They fled to join the White armies
questions.explain: The Romanov family were shot by the Bolsheviks at Ekaterinburg in July 1918 during the Civil War.

questions.q: In which year did Lenin die, triggering a struggle for the leadership?
questions.explain: Lenin died in January 1924, beginning a power struggle from which Stalin eventually emerged victorious over Trotsky.

questions.q: How did Stalin's role as General Secretary help him win the leadership struggle?
options: It let him appoint his supporters to key positions in the party
It gave him command of the Red Army
It made him head of the secret police
It allowed him to control foreign policy
questions.explain: As General Secretary, Stalin controlled party appointments, packing important posts with loyal supporters to outmanoeuvre his rivals.

questions.q: What did collectivisation involve?
options: Merging peasants' land into large state-controlled collective farms
Giving peasants private ownership of their farms
Closing all farms and importing food
questions.explain: Collectivisation combined small peasant holdings into large collective farms (kolkhozes) under state control to boost and seize grain output.

questions.q: Who were the 'kulaks' who were targeted during collectivisation?
options: Wealthier peasants who owned more land
Officers of the old Tsarist army
questions.explain: Kulaks were relatively well-off peasants; Stalin blamed them for resistance to collectivisation and 'liquidated' them as a class.

questions.q: What was the main priority of the First Five-Year Plan (1928-1932)?
options: Developing heavy industry such as coal, iron and steel
Producing consumer goods like clothing and radios
Increasing the export of luxury goods
questions.explain: The First Five-Year Plan concentrated on heavy industry, dramatically raising output of coal, iron, steel and oil.

questions.q: During the late 1930s, leading Old Bolsheviks confessed to invented crimes in public Moscow trials before being executed. This was part of which of Stalin's policies?
questions.explain: The show trials of 1936-38 were part of Stalin's purges, or Great Terror, which removed and executed rivals and 'enemies' across society.
